"authors": "Jing Fang; Tianzuo Li; Jiyeon Lee; Dahye Lim; Lianjie Xu; Yajie Liu; Jongcheol Seo; Wen-Bin Zhang",
"field_subfield": "Protein engineering / synthetic biology",
"type_of_paper": "Research article (design and synthesis of a novel protein topology)",
"executive_summary": "Proteins are normally built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional topology can enhance stability. Artificial topological proteins have been made, but they usually contain multiple domains, which complicates the study of topological effects. The authors hypothesized that a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of chemical topology. They designed and synthesized a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), consisting of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically. The design rewired the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original DHFR fold itself as the entangling template. Synthesis was achieved in Escherichia coli cells using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to a linear control (l-DHFR), cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability but with reduced activity (~5 U/mg versus ~14 U/mg), and exhibits enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The results suggest that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science, demonstrating that the chemical topology of a protein domain can be changed without collapsing the fold and bringing profound changes in properties. The study provides a new scaffold for further engineering and evolution, and opens the possibility of converting linear proteins into single-domain catenanes with identical composition to the wild-type.",

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang; Tianzuo Li; Jiyeon Lee; Dahye Lim; Lianjie Xu; Yajie Liu; Jongcheol Seo; Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (design and synthesis of a novel protein topology)
summary.executive_summary: Proteins are normally built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional topology can enhance stability. Artificial topological proteins have been made, but they usually contain multiple domains, which complicates the study of topological effects. The authors hypothesized that a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of chemical topology. They designed and synthesized a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), consisting of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically. The design rewired the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original DHFR fold itself as the entangling template. Synthesis was achieved in Escherichia coli cells using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to a linear control (l-DHFR), cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability but with reduced activity (~5 U/mg versus ~14 U/mg), and exhibits enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The results suggest that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science, demonstrating that the chemical topology of a protein domain can be changed without collapsing the fold and bringing profound changes in properties. The study provides a new scaffold for further engineering and evolution, and opens the possibility of converting linear proteins into single-domain catenanes with identical composition to the wild-type.

Most artificial topological proteins contain multiple domains. Multiple domains complicate the study of topological effects. A single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact. Single-domain topological proteins remain challenging to prepare. DHFR tolerates rethreading and retains similar structure and function.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a single-domain protein catenane be designed and synthesized? Can DHFR be converted into its single-domain catenane counterpart? Can chemical topology be changed without collapsing the fold?
